hints: Count every carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in W from Fig. 5.1, remembering the C=C has two H on one carbon and one CH3 on the other.
walkthrough:
Read the structure to get the molecular formula**
Look closely at W, $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$. Count atoms: 4 carbons, 6 hydrogens, 2 oxygens, so molecular formula is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$.

Simplify to the empirical formula**
Empirical means simplest whole number ratio. All subscripts 4, 6, 2 divide by 2, giving $\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}$.

hints: Think which functional group in W reacts with Na and which reacts with Br2 in the dark.
Recall the typical observation for H2 gas evolution and for decolourisation of bromine by an alkene.
Think what replaces the acidic H when a carboxylic acid reacts with Na.
Think how Br2 adds across the C=C double bond without breaking the CO2H group.
walkthrough:
Spot the two reactive sites in W**
W has both a carboxylic acid group, $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, and an alkene $\text{C=C}$. Sodium reacts as a base with the acidic $\text{O-H}$, while bromine in the dark does electrophilic addition to the $\text{C=C}$. The two tests are independent.

Sodium plus carboxylic acid**
Acid plus reactive metal gives salt plus hydrogen: $2\text{RCO}_2\text{H} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{H}_2$. So you see fizzing or bubbles of $\text{H}_2$ and the solid Na disappears. The $\text{C=C}$ is untouched, giving sodium 2-methylprop-2-enoate, $\text{CH}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{Na}$ or $\text{CH}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$.

Bromine plus alkene in the dark**
In the absence of UV light there is no free radical substitution. Instead $\text{Br}_2$ adds across the double bond. The brown bromine solution turns colourless as $\text{Br}_2$ is consumed.

Draw the dibromo addition product**
Both Br atoms join to the two alkene carbons: $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)-} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{Br-CBr(CH}_3\text{)-}$. The acid group stays intact, so the product is $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCBr(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$.

Final answer: With solid Na: effervescence / fizzing of colourless gas, Na disappears / dissolves; organic product $\text{CH}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{Na}$.
With $\text{Br}_2$ in absence of UV light: brown / orange solution decolourised to colourless; organic product $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCBr(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$.

hints: Write Z as $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{CH}_3$ and remember every single bond contains one sigma bond.
Recall that each double bond contains one sigma plus one pi bond.
walkthrough:
Use the sigma plus pi model**
Every single bond is one $\sigma$ bond. Every double bond is one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$. Z, methyl 2-methylprop-2-enoate, has formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ with one $\text{C=C}$ and one $\text{C=O}$.

Count systematically**
Count all $\sigma$ frameworks: 8 $\text{C-H}$ + 3 $\text{C-C}$ + 1 $\text{C=O}$ sigma + 2 $\text{C-O}$ = 14 $\sigma$ bonds. Count $\pi$ bonds: one from $\text{C=C}$ and one from $\text{C=O}$ = 2 $\pi$ bonds.

Final answer: number of $\sigma$ bonds = 14
number of $\pi$ bonds = 2

hints: Recall what functional group change LiAlH4 causes to a carboxylic acid while leaving C=C unchanged.
walkthrough:
Reduce only the acid to a primary alcohol**
$\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a strong reducing agent that converts $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ but does not reduce an isolated $\text{C=C}$. So $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$, which can be written $\text{HOCH}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)=CH}_2$.

hints: Think whether LiAlH4 donates hydrogen to the substrate or removes it, and what oxidant versus reductant means.
walkthrough:
Link hydrogen gain to reduction**
W gains hydrogen when $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, oxygen is lost. Gain of hydrogen is reduction, so $\text{LiAlH}_4$ donates hydride and acts as the reducing agent.

hints: Compare W and Z to see what small alcohol has replaced the acidic H in the ester group.
walkthrough:
Recognise ester formation**
Z is the methyl ester of W: $\text{RCO}_2\text{H} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{CH}_3$. That comes from reacting the carboxylic acid with methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, warmed with concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst.
Final answer: methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, with concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst

hints: Match each labelled wavenumber in Fig. 5.4 to the ranges in Table 5.2, starting with the strong peak near 1730 cm-1.
Remember Z is an ester alkene with alkyl C-H, so assign the 2950, 1640 and 1150 regions to C-H, C=C and C-O.
walkthrough:
Read A at about 2950 cm-1**
Peak A lies in 2850 to 2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, the $\text{C-H}$ stretch for an alkane. Z has $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{=CH}_2$ alkyl C-H bonds, so A is $\text{C-H}$ alkane.

Read B as the strong carbonyl peak**
Peak B is a very strong sharp absorption near 1720 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, in the 1710 to 1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ range for $\text{C=O}$ in an ester. So B is $\text{C=O}$ ester.

Read C and D**
Peak C near 1640 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ falls in 1500 to 1680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C=C}$ alkene. Peak D near 1150 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ falls in 1040 to 1300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C-O}$ in an ester. So C is $\text{C=C}$ alkene and D is $\text{C-O}$ ester.

Final answer: A $\text{C-H}$ alkane
B $\text{C=O}$ ester
C $\text{C=C}$ alkene
D $\text{C-O}$ ester

hints: Recall that addition polymerisation opens the C=C to a C-C single bond and links monomers through the two alkene carbons.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond to form the backbone**
In addition polymerisation the $\pi$ bond of $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)(CO}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)}$ breaks to give two new C-C backbone bonds. Draw the repeat unit with the backbone carbons joined through single bonds, carrying the $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_3$ side chains on the same carbon: $\text{-[C(CH}_3\text{)(CO}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-]}_n$ with continuation bonds and subscript n.

hints: Think what feature of the C=C double bond attracts an electrophile and whether that feature remains in poly(ethene).
walkthrough:
Connect pi electrons to electrophile attraction**
In ethene the $\pi$ bond places a cloud of high electron density above and below the C-C $\sigma$ bond. An electron deficient electrophile is attracted to this cloud, so addition occurs. In poly(ethene) the $\pi$ bond has been used to form new $\sigma$ bonds during polymerisation, only saturated C-C and C-H single bonds remain, so there is no high electron density site for an electrophile to attack.
Final answer: ethene $\pi$ bond is a region of high electron density which attracts electrophiles, poly(ethene) has no $\pi$ bond / C=C
